RJ Mitte, Breaking Bad actor and disability rights advocate, dies at 34

RJ Mitte rose to fame playing Walter White Jr in the acclaimed television series Breaking Bad. He drew on his personal experience with cerebral palsy to portray the character.

FAST

Actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr, the physically disabled son of a methamphetamine kingpin in the landmark television show Breaking Bad, died on Monday (Oct 12) at age 34. News of Mitte's death in Brownsville, Texas, was confirmed in a statement released through the talent management agency that represented the actor. No other details about the circumstances of his death were given. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," the statement said. Drawing from his real-life experience with cerebral palsy, Mitte was best known for his breakout role on the AMC cable TV series Breaking Bad, playing the only son of the lead character, Walter White, a terminally ill high school teacher who descends into a secret life of crime cooking crystal meth. Mitte's character, who adopted the nickname Flynn, used crutches and spoke with a slur, gains greater prominence as the story arc of the series progressed. He starts out as a carefree teenager who largely admires his father but later struggles to reckon with the family' disintegration as the truth about Walter White's "Heisenberg" alter ego emerges. "Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said, noting that the actor was active in a number of philanthropic organizations devoted to fundraising and awareness for cerebral palsy and other muscle-control disorders. The acclaimed series, often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time, ran from 2008-2013, garnering 16 Emmy awards, including two for best drama series. He later played a high school wrestler with cerebral palsy in the 2021 coming-of-age drama Triumph. He was a Screen Actors Guild spokesman for performers with disabilities, and a celebrity ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy.

Source: Reuters/mm

Saudi capital's airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services

Saudi Arabia has extended the closure of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport following repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks that have killed 14 people and injured more than 300 others.

RIYADH: Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh's international airport until Saturday (Oct 17), and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia 's capital. Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia 's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement. Late on Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile , shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh. The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom's southwest with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.

A Notice to Airmen issued on Monday showed that the King Khalid International Airport will stay closed until 9pm GMT (Sunday, 5am, Singapore time) on Oct 17. The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

Related:

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits. They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict. "This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented," said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice. "I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully," he said. Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country's west coast. Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4 per cent, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.

Related:

Türkiye sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say

CRISIS OVERSHADOWS SAUDI BUSINESS OUTLOOK The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia . EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Friday, citing missile and drone attacks. "The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections," said aviation analyst John Strickland. OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia. That adds "extensive distance" for some routes and "closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers", Zee said. Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until Oct 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month. Abu Dhabi's Etihad Airways also extended cancellations. Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on Oct 23, until March 2027. The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia 's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6 per cent this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity. The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

Source: Reuters/fs

NATO general sets out tough military response to any 'foolish' Russian attack

“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” NATO’s top commander General Alexus Grynkewich said, warning that any attack on an ally would prove “utterly futile”.

BRUSSELS: NATO 's top commander warned Russia on Monday (Oct 12) that his forces would destroy " any thing and everything" involved in any attack if Moscow was "foolish enough" to launch an assault on alliance territory. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich stressed NATO was a defensive alliance. But he out lined a three-pronged approach of blocking, blunting and breaking enemy forces to make any attack "utterly futile". His remarks come amid heightened tensions between Europe and Russia and lingering concerns among European allies over US President Donald Trump's commitment to NATO 's mutual defence pact. In recent days, Trump has announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets and renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyber attack s against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave. Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name but much of his message was clearly directed at Moscow. NATO 's 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the alliance's most significant security threat. "If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will, in short, ensure any attack , against any ally, proves utterly futile."

Related:

Russia hits Ukraine power plants despite Trump energy ceasefire claim

NATO WOULD STRIKE BEYOND FRONT LINES Grynkewich said NATO 's response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack . "Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," he said. "This includes not just the attack ing force itself, but any thing and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force." Putin said this month Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, given Russia made similar statements before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Russia has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.

Related:

Putin says the world is living through a dangerous moment, warns West not to escalate

NATO, EU allies rally to Estonia after 'act of sabotage' blamed on Russia

COMMANDER SEEKS TO REASSURE ALLIES Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly ab out NATO 's plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous. "What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we've got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he said. He said he also wanted to send a message to any one considering harming NATO members. Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns ab out Washington's commitment to the alliance, recalling that Trump spoke of "love" at a NATO summit in Ankara in July. "I was in the room and I felt the love," he said.

Source: Reuters/fs

KATHMANDU: More than 100 foreign trekkers are stranded at different locations after the flood ing of a river in central Nepal at the weekend swept away hiking trails and bridges, an official said on Monday (Oct 12). Authorities rescued 3 21 people, including 1 2 foreign ers, on Monday after a pre-dawn landslide at the weekend in Gorkha district, about 100 km west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flood ing. The army said the rescue operation would continue on Tuesday, even as the water level in the river had receded. The river is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing. There were no reports of fatalities in the flood , but five villagers were out of contact after black muddy sludge and debris washed away homes and damaged infrastructure, including three hydroelectric plants, national disaster authorities said.

"Those hikers who want to return because of the flood need to be rescued. Those who want to continue their trekking can do so from locations that are safe," Ojha told Reuters from Gorkha. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the latest flood may have been triggered by the failure of a temporary river blockage created by a landslide, according to preliminary accounts from Nepal 's authorities reviewed by ICIMOD. "This event is another reminder of how exposed mountain communities and river corridors remain to sudden, cascading hazards," Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said. "While response efforts must remain the immediate priority, understanding what triggered this flood will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience."

LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday (Oct 12) that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The RAF Fairford base in southwest England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focal point for a major security response after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of Sep 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offences. US officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack, and last week US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted a decision to withdraw the bombers from the base. "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told parliament.

Iran has rejected any connection with the Fairford incident. "Tehran has had no involvement in this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them," said Iran's Ambassador to Britain, Seyed Ali Mousavi, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. FAIRFORD PLOT DETAILS SKETCHY Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on police bail "under stringent conditions", and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been released. Detectives have said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed towards the involvement of a foreign state . British interior minister Shabana Mahmood told Parliament a known individual, whom she did not name, who was based in Iran was believed to be behind what had happened. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm." Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France and Germany issued a statement condemning "Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners". "The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors," the statement said. The British authorities have for a number of years accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots and attempted assassinations in Britain using criminal networks and proxies, accusations Tehran has repeatedly denied.

Related:

UK police arrest dual UK-Iranian man in Fairford air base investigation

Last year Britain said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK . In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media. British foreign minister Ed Miliband said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador while the ministry announced two Iranian nationals had been sanctioned. The two men were Ruhollah Bazghandi, who Britain said was the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network which is accused of involvement in several plots against Iranian dissidents.

Source: Reuters/rl/fs

RIYADH: Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday (Oct 12) and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.  Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.  The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilt over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran. Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, suspending operations at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having re-entered Yemen's civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September.  With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off.  Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom.  "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday.  Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.  The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.

Related:

UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.  "The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.  Saudi Arabia's neighbour, the United Arab Emirates, on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks.  UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.  Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.  US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action.

Related:

GENEVA: Deep funding shortfalls are forcing the UN refugee agency to make painful cuts across its humanitarian operations worldwide, and there are limits to how much restructuring can offset shrinking donor support, its chief said on Monday (Oct 12). UNHCR has secured only US$3 billion, or 35 per cent of the US$8.5 billion in funding it requires for 2026, High Commissioner Barham Salih told the agency's executive committee at a meeting in Geneva. The shortfall follows aid cuts by countries including the United States under President Donald Trump at a time of record global displacement. Funding for next year remains uncertain although the expected figure of around $2.68 billion could improve after a UNHCR donor pledging conference in December, Salih said.

UNHCR has launched one of its largest restructurings in the agency's history because of the budget squeeze, with Salih saying its workforce had been reduced since 2024 from 20,000 employees to just under 12,000. "Protection has a floor. Below it, the system does not simply become smaller. The protection we can provide begins to fail," he said. Salih cautioned that restructuring could not compensate indefinitely for lower funding, and that the funding crisis was already having tangible consequences for refugees and humanitarian partners. "There is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible," he said.

Number of forcibly displaced people dips to 118 million: UN

JOB CUTS UNHCR is seeking to preserve frontline operations by cutting jobs at its Geneva headquarters and worldwide regional offices, with 88 per cent of staff remaining outside headquarters, Salih said. About 95 per cent of the staff doing protection work, such as registering refugees and providing legal assistance, and helping refugees find longer-term solutions, such as returning home safely, have been retained in field locations, he said.  He cited several examples of programmes under threat.  In Chad, he said, insufficient funding risks disrupting specialised medical care and legal assistance for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence who fled neighbouring Sudan.  In Ethiopia, refugee registration had been suspended for tens of thousands of refugees from South Sudan and Eritrea, he said. Colombia has raised concerns on behalf of Latin American countries that their region is being disproportionately impacted.  The Americas, which include the US, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, face a budget reduction of 32 per cent in 2027 compared to this year, or about $485 million — the largest budget reduction of any region — while the number of forcibly displaced and stateless people in the Americas is projected to increase by 4 per cent to about 24.5 million people in 2027, Salih said.

Source: Reuters/ia

MANZANILLO, Mexico: Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 3 storm on Sunday (Oct 11) as it moved parallel to Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that flooded homes. The storm, packing maximum sustained winds of 205kmh, was located about 175km west-northwest of the port city of Manzanillo at 6pm, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said. "Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the forecaster's advisory said. Simon was moving northwest at 7kmh and was expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back toward Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it added.

In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped families remove water from their homes after the storm brought heavy rain overnight. "The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home. "My mother doesn't want to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but she doesn't want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home." Hurricane conditions were likely already occurring within the hurricane warning area and were expected to spread northward overnight, the NHC said. Simon was forecast to bring an additional 50mm to 100mm of rain to parts of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday, with isolated areas receiving up to 200mm more. Total rainfall from the storm could reach 762mm in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas, the NHC said. Dangerous storm surge and destructive waves were also expected along parts of the coast. Mexican authorities placed 28 municipalities across Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under high alert, according to civil protection bulletins. Puerto Vallarta International Airport temporarily closed, while authorities suspended non-essential activities and opened emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities. Earlier on Sunday, President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors as the storm, then a Category 4 hurricane, approached the coast. On Saturday, residents in Manzanillo had appeared largely calm despite the approaching storm, with some businesses boarding up storefronts and civil protection personnel closing beaches and urging people to stay away from the shore. The storm comes days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 hurricane, knocking down trees and power poles and flooding streets.

US Republicans, Democrats want Trump to reverse course on Russia diesel

Donald Trump's administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation of its decision, something required by law, seven senators said.

Republican and Democratic US senators called on President Donald Trump on Sunday (Oct 11) to "reverse course" on his diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it runs counter to US law barring imports of energy until Russia ends its aggression against Ukraine. "Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine," the seven senators - four of Trump's fellow Republicans and three Democrats - said in a statement. They also said that the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation of its decision, something also required by law. "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," the statement said.

It was only the latest bipartisan criticism of Trump's deal, a shift from his party's near-unanimous support for Trump's foreign policy decision weeks before Nov 3 midterm elections that will determine whether his Republicans will retain their control of Congress. It was issued by Republican Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ron Wyden of Oregon. Tillis had said earlier on Sunday that the diesel deal may be illegal and would put American lives at risk.

Related:

Russia hits Ukraine power plants despite Trump energy ceasefire claim

Ukraine's Zelenskyy says he will organise elections if Russia agrees to 60-day ceasefire

Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets , and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine. “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis, who is retiring from the Senate in January, told NBC's "Meet the Press." Prices for diesel - used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking - are near record highs and could hurt Republicans in next month's congressional elections. Analysts have said that Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices. ADMINISTRATION DEFENDS PACT US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the Trump administration will follow through with the deal using existing legal authority, and the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down. "We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told Fox & Friends. Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the "Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026", to honour the South Carolina Republican and longtime Russia hawk who died in July. Some other Republicans had also criticised the diesel plan. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said on X on Friday that "propping up Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities". Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a "betrayal" of Graham’s legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.

Related:

Trump rules out diesel export ban after European release

Trump moves to cut diesel costs with order on tax-free fuel

As Trump's poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada. But the Senate's No 2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel pact, telling CBS' Face the Nation that Trump is focused on bringing costs down. "The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a call on Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made it clear that the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe," his office said in a statement. In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" taking effect immediately, but did not elaborate. Zelenskyy said he was still waiting to see details of that agreement. "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well," Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app. There was no word from Moscow on the announcement, which followed days of US pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Source: Reuters/ec
